PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 41 — Lesson 65: Respiratory Health Assessment & Diagnostics

FNP-level goal: Assess cough, dyspnea, wheeze, hypoxemia, and chest symptoms using a mechanism-based respiratory differential; identify respiratory compromise early; select appropriate imaging and pulmonary-function testing; and distinguish safe outpatient follow-up from emergency evaluation.

Learning Objectives

  • Construct a focused respiratory problem representation using onset, trigger, severity, exposures, comorbidities, and trajectory.
  • Recognize signs of impending respiratory failure and decide when outpatient assessment is unsafe.
  • Differentiate common patterns of upper-airway, obstructive-airway, alveolar/interstitial, pleural, vascular, cardiac, and infectious disease.
  • Use pulse oximetry, chest imaging, spirometry, peak flow, and targeted laboratory tests for specific diagnostic questions.
  • Apply a safe approach to possible asthma/COPD exacerbation, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism, and pneumothorax.
  • Create explicit return precautions and follow-up plans for respiratory illness.

Part 1 — Start With Breathing Work, Not the Diagnosis

In a respiratory complaint, assess airway, breathing, circulation, and mental status before completing a detailed history. Observe the respiratory rate, ability to speak, accessory-muscle use, posture, cyanosis, diaphoresis, agitation, fatigue, and level of consciousness. New confusion, exhaustion, silent or markedly reduced breath sounds in a distressed patient, severe work of breathing, hypoxemia, hypotension, or inability to protect the airway can signal respiratory failure or another emergency.

Do not allow a familiar label—“asthma,” “bronchitis,” “anxiety,” or “COPD”—to delay a stability assessment. A patient with a known chronic lung diagnosis can also develop pulmonary embolism, ACS, heart failure, pneumonia, pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, or sepsis. The first question is: Can this patient safely remain in an outpatient setting right now?

Part 2 — Build a Respiratory Problem Representation

Clarify onset (sudden, hours-days, weeks, chronic), trigger (exertion, infection, allergen, aspiration, travel, position, exposure), trajectory, baseline function, and associated symptoms. Ask about fever, sputum, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain, chest pressure, wheeze, stridor, orthopnea, edema, palpitations, syncope, weight change, night symptoms, reflux, nasal symptoms, and constitutional symptoms.

Context changes probability: age, pregnancy potential, smoking/vaping, occupational/environmental exposures, cancer, immobility, recent surgery, thrombosis history, immune suppression, vaccination status, known asthma/COPD/heart failure, medications, ACE-inhibitor use, aspiration risk, travel, and sick contacts are not background details. They shape the differential and urgency.

Part 3 — Cough: Classify Before Treating

Cough may be acute, subacute, or chronic. Acute cough commonly accompanies viral illness, but pneumonia, asthma/COPD exacerbation, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, aspiration, and serious infection may require consideration depending on symptoms and risk. Chronic cough can reflect upper-airway cough syndrome, asthma, GERD, ACE-inhibitor effect, chronic bronchitis/COPD, bronchiectasis, interstitial disease, malignancy, or other causes.

Ask about duration, nocturnal pattern, exertion, sputum character, blood, fever, weight loss, dysphagia/aspiration, smoking/vaping, TB or fungal exposure where relevant, medication changes, and imaging history. Hemoptysis, persistent unexplained cough, weight loss, recurrent pneumonia, hypoxemia, systemic toxicity, or significant cancer/immunologic risk requires more than empiric cough medication.

Part 4 — Dyspnea: Think Air, Blood, Pump, and Demand

Dyspnea can result from impaired airflow, impaired gas exchange, reduced oxygen delivery, increased metabolic demand, altered ventilatory drive, cardiac congestion, vascular obstruction, anemia, acid-base disturbance, neuromuscular weakness, or anxiety. Use the history and exam to organize the pattern rather than labeling all shortness of breath as “pulmonary.” Orthopnea, edema, weight gain, crackles, and a rapid irregular rhythm may point toward a cardiac contribution; sudden pleuritic pain with VTE risk may raise pulmonary-embolism concern; fever and focal findings may suggest infection; wheeze and variable triggers may support airway disease.

“Anxiety” is a diagnosis of inclusion after appropriate assessment, not a shortcut around red flags. New dyspnea, change from baseline, reduced exercise tolerance, or new oxygen requirement deserves explanation.

Part 5 — Focused Respiratory Examination

Inspect work of breathing, respiratory pattern, speech, chest symmetry, cyanosis, and mental status. Palpate for tenderness, expansion, subcutaneous emphysema, and tracheal position when clinically indicated. Percuss and auscultate systematically, comparing matching areas. Describe wheeze, crackles, breath-sound reduction, focal asymmetry, stridor, and prolonged expiration precisely. Examine heart rate/rhythm, edema, perfusion, and legs when cardiovascular or VTE disease is plausible.

Wheeze is neither necessary nor specific for asthma. It can occur with COPD, heart failure, anaphylaxis, upper-airway obstruction, foreign body, or other processes. A quiet chest in a patient who is tiring can be more concerning than loud wheeze. Crackles can be infectious, cardiogenic, interstitial, or otherwise. Physical findings update probability; they do not independently exclude serious disease.

Part 6 — Pulse Oximetry and Oxygenation: Interpret the Patient

Pulse oximetry estimates hemoglobin oxygen saturation, not ventilation, work of breathing, or total oxygen content. Confirm an unexpected value with signal quality, probe placement, perfusion, and clinical appearance in mind. A normal saturation does not rule out PE, early pneumonia, ACS, asthma, anemia, or impending fatigue. Conversely, a low value is clinically significant but must be interpreted in relation to the patient’s known baseline, chronic lung disease, and the measurement quality.

When oxygenation or ventilation failure is suspected, urgent/emergency assessment may require blood gas testing, imaging, serial reassessment, and higher-level respiratory support. These are not routine primary-care tests for a patient who is unstable. Do not delay transfer while repeatedly obtaining office measurements in a deteriorating patient.

Part 7 — Chest Imaging: What Question Are You Asking?

Chest radiography can help evaluate focal infiltrate, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, mass, and other thoracic abnormalities, but it can be normal early in some conditions and cannot independently exclude PE or every pneumonia. Use imaging to answer a clinical question and pair it with the history, examination, and disposition.

CT, CT angiography, and other advanced imaging have important indications but expose patients to radiation, contrast risk, incidental findings, and downstream testing. Do not order advanced imaging as a substitute for a focused risk assessment. For suspected PE, use a validated probability-based pathway and local protocol; for unstable patients, emergency evaluation and stabilization come first.

Part 8 — Spirometry, Peak Flow, and Airway Diagnosis

Spirometry provides objective information about airflow limitation and can support diagnosis of asthma, COPD, or other pulmonary disease when performed with acceptable technique and interpreted in clinical context. Symptoms and response to an inhaler alone are not enough to confidently label every patient with asthma or COPD. Airway disease may be episodic, and a normal test between episodes does not automatically eliminate a clinically plausible diagnosis.

Peak-flow monitoring can help selected patients follow known asthma or document variability when used consistently, but it is effort-dependent and does not replace assessment of severe symptoms. Do not send a patient with severe dyspnea, altered mental status, marked hypoxemia, silent chest, or failure to respond to rescue therapy home simply to record peak flows. For a suspected COPD diagnosis, post-bronchodilator spirometry and trained interpretation are central to confirmation.

Part 9 — High-Consequence Respiratory Differentials

Possible pneumonia: consider fever, cough, focal findings, hypoxemia, tachypnea, older age, immune compromise, and sepsis risk. Outpatient treatment may be appropriate only after evaluating severity, oxygenation, ability to take oral therapy, support, and follow-up.

Possible PE: consider sudden/unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic pain, syncope, hemoptysis, tachycardia, hypoxemia, unilateral swelling, recent immobility/surgery, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum context, prior VTE, or estrogen exposure. Physical examination cannot exclude PE. Use probability-based testing and emergency disposition when unstable.

Possible pneumothorax: sudden pleuritic pain, acute dyspnea, unilateral decreased breath sounds, trauma, or relevant risk context can require urgent imaging/emergency evaluation. Possible anaphylaxis or upper-airway obstruction: stridor, voice change, facial/tongue swelling, hives, hypotension, or rapidly progressive symptoms require immediate emergency response.

Part 10 — Follow-Up Is Part of Respiratory Safety

For an outpatient respiratory plan, document why outpatient care is appropriate, the working differential, treatment/supportive plan, expected trajectory, when results will be reviewed, and what requires same-day or emergency reassessment. Return precautions should be specific: worsening dyspnea, new chest pain, persistent fever, confusion, fainting, hemoptysis, inability to hydrate or take medication, cyanosis, decreased urine output, or failure to improve as expected.

Reassess when the illness does not behave as predicted. A patient returning with worsening symptoms has new diagnostic data; do not simply repeat the original label or prescription without rebuilding the problem representation.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: “Just an Asthma Flare”

A 34-year-old with asthma develops progressive dyspnea after a viral illness. They are speaking in short phrases, using accessory muscles, and have markedly reduced air movement with minimal wheeze.

FNP reasoning: the quiet chest and increased work of breathing may indicate severe airflow limitation and fatigue, not improvement. Assess immediate stability and arrange emergency care rather than continuing a routine inhaler-refill discussion.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Cough, Fever, and a Safe Outpatient Plan

A stable 42-year-old has five days of cough, fever, focal crackles, normal mentation, stable oxygenation, and can take fluids and medication. They have no major comorbidity and reliable follow-up.

FNP reasoning: evaluate for pneumonia severity and alternatives, use targeted testing/imaging when indicated, and ensure a clear plan. Outpatient care is not “no follow-up”: document return precautions and the expected trajectory.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Sudden Dyspnea After Travel

A 58-year-old develops sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain after prolonged travel; their calf is newly swollen. The office lung examination is not remarkable.

FNP reasoning: a normal lung examination does not eliminate PE. The acute timing and VTE context require immediate probability-based evaluation and disposition based on stability, not empiric treatment for anxiety or bronchitis.

FNP Respiratory-Assessment Framework

  1. Assess stability first: work of breathing, ability to speak, mental status, oxygenation context, perfusion, and fatigue.
  2. Define the pattern: cough, acute/chronic dyspnea, wheeze, pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, or upper-airway symptoms.
  3. Build the differential: airway, alveolar/interstitial, pleural, vascular, cardiac, infectious, hematologic, metabolic, and medication-related causes.
  4. Examine purposefully: compare lung fields, evaluate respiratory effort, and include cardiovascular/VTE clues when indicated.
  5. Test with a question: pulse oximetry, chest imaging, spirometry/peak flow, targeted labs, or probability-based VTE testing.
  6. Respect limitations: normal saturation, normal early imaging, or normal office spirometry does not always exclude serious or episodic disease.
  7. Choose disposition and safety-net: emergency care for instability; explicit return precautions for stable outpatient care.

High-Yield Summary

Dyspnea: think airway, gas exchange, vascular, cardiac pump, oxygen delivery, metabolic demand, and neurologic/psychologic contributors.
Wheeze: is a clue, not a diagnosis; a quiet chest in severe distress can be dangerous.
Pulse oximetry: estimates saturation, not ventilation or the entire severity picture.
Chest x-ray: answers selected structural questions but does not exclude every serious thoracic diagnosis.
Spirometry: supports objective asthma/COPD assessment when technique and timing are appropriate.
PE/pneumothorax/anaphylaxis: require rapid recognition and appropriate urgent/emergency pathways.
FNP standard: never let a familiar respiratory label delay stability assessment, probability-based testing, or escalation.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Respiratory assessment, oxygen therapy, spirometry, imaging, emergency triage, treatment, referral, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
